\chapter{Eight Verbs at the Core}
\label{ch:la-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{37}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I am, I have, I go, I come, I say, I see, I know and I give in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, and name the English words each verb left behind.}

The chapter's eighth verb closes the set: after learning dō, the reader produces all eight first-person forms and all eight third-person forms in sequence — sum, habeō, eō, veniō, dīcō, videō, sciō, dō and est, habet, it, venit, dīcit, videt, scit, dat.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sum, esse]{sum — the verb English never stopped sharing}

\label{lesson:LA-C37-sum}



\begin{quote}
You can already say \textbf{valeō}, \textquotedblleft{}I fare well.\textquotedblright{} Now meet the verb that sits under every such statement: \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sum — \textquotedblleft{}I am\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Sum} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I am}.\textquotedblright{} The form a dictionary lists it under is \textbf{esse}, \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{sum} — I am
  \item \textbf{es} — you are, to one person
  \item \textbf{est} — he is, she is, it is
  \item \textbf{sumus} — we are
  \item \textbf{estis} — you are, to several people
  \item \textbf{sunt} — they are
\end{itemize}

Latin packs the person into the ending, so \textbf{sum} on its own is already a whole sentence. No separate word for \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} is required.

\begin{cousinweb}
Two English words are not merely cousins of these forms — they are the same inherited word. \textbf{Am} and \textbf{is} come from the Proto-Indo-European root \emph{\textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}es-}} (\textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}), and so do \textbf{sum} and \textbf{est}.

Latin builds its past from a second root entirely: \textbf{fuī} (\textquotedblleft{}I was\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{futūrus} (\textquotedblleft{}about to be\textquotedblright{}) come from \emph{\textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}uH-}} (\textquotedblleft{}to grow, become\textquotedblright{}) — which also gives English \textbf{be} and \textbf{been}, and Greek \emph{phúsis} (\textquotedblleft{}nature\textquotedblright{}), the source of \textbf{physics}. English patches its own verb from three roots the same way: \emph{am/is}, \emph{be}, and \emph{was/were}.

From \textbf{esse} Latin built \textbf{essentia}, giving English \textbf{essence} and \textbf{essential}. Its participle \emph{-sēns} supplies \textbf{present} (\emph{prae-}, \textquotedblleft{}before\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{absent} (\emph{ab-}, \textquotedblleft{}away\textquotedblright{}), while the phrase \emph{inter est} (\textquotedblleft{}it is between, it matters\textquotedblright{}) hardened into \textbf{interest}.

Flag one false friend: Latin \textbf{sum} has nothing to do with an English \textquotedblleft{}sum.\textquotedblright{} That word comes from \emph{summa}, \textquotedblleft{}the highest, the total.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sum\textquotedblright{} — I am
  \item \textquotedblleft{}es, est\textquotedblright{} — you are, he or she is
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sumus, estis, sunt\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the two English forms of the same root — am, is
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I am\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Sum}.) \textquotedblleft{}They are\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Sunt}.) What form does a dictionary list? (\textbf{Esse}.) Which two English words come from the very same root as \emph{sum} and \emph{est}? (\textbf{Am} and \textbf{is}.) Where does Latin's past \textbf{fuī} come from instead? (\textbf{A second root, *b\textsuperscript{h}uH-, which also gives English \emph{be}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[habeō, habēre]{habeō — the twin that is not a twin}

\label{lesson:LA-C37-habeo}



\begin{quote}
You can say \textbf{sum}, \textquotedblleft{}I am.\textquotedblright{} The next verb says what you hold. It resembles its English translation so closely that the resemblance is a trap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: habeō — \textquotedblleft{}I have\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Habeō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I have},\textquotedblright{} and more literally \textquotedblleft{}I hold.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{habēre}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{habeō} — I have
  \item \textbf{habēs} — you have, to one person
  \item \textbf{habet} — he has, she has, it has
  \item \textbf{habēmus} — we have
  \item \textbf{habētis} — you have, to several people
  \item \textbf{habent} — they have
\end{itemize}

The \emph{h} was already weak in everyday Roman speech, and every Romance descendant dropped it: the letter is written, barely breathed.

\begin{cousinweb}
Here is the trap. English \textbf{have} is \textbf{not} descended from \emph{habēre}. It comes from the Proto-Indo-European root \emph{\textbf{*keh\textsubscript{2}p-}} (\textquotedblleft{}to seize\textquotedblright{}), whose Latin outcome is \textbf{capere} — the verb behind \textbf{capture}, \textbf{captive}, and \textbf{capable}. Two languages, two unrelated verbs, one accidental match of sound and sense. Etymologists cite this pair as the standard warning against trusting a resemblance.

The genuine English family of \emph{habēre} is large. From \emph{habitus} (\textquotedblleft{}condition, bearing\textquotedblright{}) come \textbf{habit} and \textbf{habitual}; from \emph{habitāre} (\textquotedblleft{}to keep having, to dwell\textquotedblright{}) come \textbf{inhabit} and \textbf{habitat}. Prefixed, the verb yields \textbf{exhibit} (\textquotedblleft{}hold out\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{prohibit} (\textquotedblleft{}hold away\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{inhibit}. The adjective \emph{habilis} (\textquotedblleft{}easily held, handy\textquotedblright{}) passes through French into \textbf{able} and \textbf{ability}. And \emph{dē} + \emph{habēre} — \textquotedblleft{}to have from someone\textquotedblright{} — contracts to \textbf{dēbēre}, which supplies \textbf{debt}, \textbf{debit}, \textbf{due}, and \textbf{duty}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}habeō\textquotedblright{} — I have
  \item \textquotedblleft{}habēs, habet\textquotedblright{} — you have, he or she has
  \item \textquotedblleft{}habēmus, habētis, habent\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — habit, inhabit, exhibit, able, debt
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I have\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Habeō}.) \textquotedblleft{}They have\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Habent}.) Is English \emph{have} descended from \emph{habēre}? (\textbf{No} — it comes from the root behind Latin \emph{capere}, \textquotedblleft{}to seize\textquotedblright{}.) Which English word hides \emph{dē} + \emph{habēre}? (\textbf{Debt}, and with it \emph{debit} and \emph{due}.) Which everyday word comes from \emph{habilis}, \textquotedblleft{}handy\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Able}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eō, īre]{eō — a whole verb in one vowel}

\label{lesson:LA-C37-eo}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Habeō} gave you a comfortable two-syllable stem. The next verb has almost no stem at all — and you have been reading one of its forms in English theatres your whole life.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: eō — \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Eō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I go}.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{īre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go.\textquotedblright{} Strip the endings and what remains is a single vowel, \emph{i-}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{eō} — I go
  \item \textbf{īs} — you go, to one person
  \item \textbf{it} — he goes, she goes, it goes
  \item \textbf{īmus} — we go
  \item \textbf{ītis} — you go, to several people
  \item \textbf{eunt} — they go
\end{itemize}

Two cautions worth hearing once. Latin \textbf{it} means \textquotedblleft{}he or she goes\textquotedblright{} and has no connection to English \textquotedblleft{}it.\textquotedblright{} And the long \emph{ī} of \textbf{īs} is a held vowel, which is what keeps it distinct from other short words.

\begin{cousinweb}
The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}ey-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to go.\textquotedblright{} Latin prefixed it relentlessly, and English took the results wholesale.

\textbf{Exit} is not derived from a Latin verb — it \emph{is} one: \emph{exit}, \textquotedblleft{}he or she goes out,\textquotedblright{} borrowed straight from Roman stage directions. Alongside it come \textbf{transit} and \textbf{transient} (\emph{trāns}, \textquotedblleft{}across\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{initial} and \textbf{initiate} (\emph{in-īre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go in,\textquotedblright{} hence \emph{initium}, \textquotedblleft{}a beginning\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{perish} (\emph{per-īre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go away utterly\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{circuit} (\emph{circum}, \textquotedblleft{}around\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{obituary} (\emph{ob-īre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go to meet\textquotedblright{} one's death).

Two are less obvious. \textbf{Ambition} is \emph{ambīre}, \textquotedblleft{}to go around\textquotedblright{} — what a Roman candidate did, walking the city to canvass for votes. \textbf{Sudden} is \emph{subitus}, from \emph{sub-īre}, \textquotedblleft{}to come up from underneath,\textquotedblright{} unnoticed until it arrives. The related noun \emph{iter}, \emph{itineris} (\textquotedblleft{}a journey\textquotedblright{}), gives \textbf{itinerary}.

Beyond Latin, the Greek participle \emph{ión} (\textquotedblleft{}going\textquotedblright{}) was borrowed by Michael Faraday in 1834 to name a particle that travels through a solution: \textbf{ion}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eō\textquotedblright{} — I go
  \item \textquotedblleft{}īs, it\textquotedblright{} — you go, he or she goes
  \item \textquotedblleft{}īmus, ītis, eunt\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — exit, transit, initial, perish, sudden
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Eō}.) \textquotedblleft{}They go\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Eunt}.) What does Latin \textbf{it} mean? (\textbf{He or she goes} — not English \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{}.) Which English stage direction is an untouched Latin verb form? (\textbf{Exit}.) What did a Roman candidate literally do to earn the word \textbf{ambition}? (\textbf{Go around}, canvassing the city.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[veniō, venīre]{veniō — the one that really is English \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:LA-C37-venio}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Eō} takes you away. Its opposite number brings you in — and this time the English translation genuinely is the same ancient word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: veniō — \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Veniō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I come}.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{venīre}. Remember that Latin \emph{v} is pronounced like English \emph{w}, so this opens \emph{weh-}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{veniō} — I come
  \item \textbf{venīs} — you come, to one person
  \item \textbf{venit} — he comes, she comes, it comes
  \item \textbf{venīmus} — we come
  \item \textbf{venītis} — you come, to several people
  \item \textbf{veniunt} — they come
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*g\textsuperscript{w}em-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to step, to come.\textquotedblright{} That initial \emph{g\textsuperscript{w}} hardens to \emph{k} in the Germanic branch, which is exactly how English \textbf{come} arises — so \emph{veniō} and \emph{come} are the same word, split apart several thousand years ago. In the Greek branch the root became \emph{baínō}, \textquotedblleft{}I step,\textquotedblright{} which supplies \textbf{base}, \textbf{basis}, and \textbf{acrobat} (\textquotedblleft{}one who walks on tiptoe\textquotedblright{}).

The Latin branch is where English got rich. Prefixed, \emph{venīre} produces \textbf{advent} and \textbf{adventure} (\emph{ad}, \textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{convene}, \textbf{convenient} and \textbf{convent} (\emph{con-}, \textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{} — what is convenient literally \textquotedblleft{}comes together\textquotedblright{} well), \textbf{event} (\emph{ē-}, \textquotedblleft{}out\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{invent} (\emph{in-}, \textquotedblleft{}to come upon\textquotedblright{} — an inventor originally \emph{found} rather than made), \textbf{prevent} (\emph{prae-}, \textquotedblleft{}to come before\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{intervene}, and \textbf{revenue} (\emph{re-}, \textquotedblleft{}what comes back\textquotedblright{}). Through French come \textbf{avenue}, \textbf{venue}, and \textbf{souvenir} (\emph{subvenīre}, \textquotedblleft{}to come to mind\textquotedblright{}).

Flag a false friend: \textbf{Venus}, \textbf{venerate}, and \textbf{venom} look like members of this family and are not. They belong to a separate root, \emph{\textbf{*wenh\textsubscript{1}-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to desire\textquotedblright{} — the same one that gives English \textbf{win} and \textbf{wish}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}veniō\textquotedblright{} — I come, with a w-sound
  \item \textquotedblleft{}venīs, venit\textquotedblright{} — you come, he or she comes
  \item \textquotedblleft{}venīmus, venītis, veniunt\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — advent, convenient, invent, revenue
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Veniō}, opening with a w-sound.) \textquotedblleft{}They come\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Veniunt}.) Which everyday English verb is the same inherited word? (\textbf{Come}.) What does \textbf{invent} literally mean? (\textbf{To come upon}, to find.) Do \textbf{Venus} and \textbf{venom} belong to this family? (\textbf{No} — a separate root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to desire\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dīcō, dīcere]{dīcō — saying began as pointing}

\label{lesson:LA-C37-dico}



\begin{quote}
You know \textbf{valē}, the farewell from Chapter 1. Learn the verb for \textquotedblleft{}say,\textquotedblright{} and one of English's grandest school words falls open.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dīcō — \textquotedblleft{}I say\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Dīcō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I say}\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}I tell.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{dīcere}. The \emph{c} is always hard, as in English \textquotedblleft{}keep,\textquotedblright{} so this is \emph{DEE-koh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{dīcō} — I say
  \item \textbf{dīcis} — you say, to one person
  \item \textbf{dīcit} — he says, she says
  \item \textbf{dīcimus} — we say
  \item \textbf{dīcitis} — you say, to several people
  \item \textbf{dīcunt} — they say
\end{itemize}

Latin also had a near-twin with a short \emph{i}, \textbf{dicāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to proclaim formally, to consecrate.\textquotedblright{} That sibling — not \emph{dīcere} itself — is where \textbf{dedicate} and \textbf{abdicate} come from.

\begin{cousinweb}
The Proto-Indo-European root \emph{\textbf{*dey\'{k}-}} meant \textquotedblleft{}to point out, to show.\textquotedblright{} Saying is a late specialisation of showing, and the family keeps both senses visible.

Pointing survives in \textbf{index} (\textquotedblleft{}the pointer,\textquotedblright{} which is also the name of the forefinger) and \textbf{indicate}. Saying dominates the rest: \textbf{dictate}, \textbf{dictator}, \textbf{dictionary}, \textbf{diction}, \textbf{edict}, \textbf{predict}, \textbf{contradict}, and \textbf{benediction} (\textquotedblleft{}speaking well\textquotedblright{}). A \textbf{verdict} is \emph{vērē dictum}, \textquotedblleft{}truly said.\textquotedblright{} A \textbf{judge} is a \emph{iūdex}, from \emph{iūs} (\textquotedblleft{}law\textquotedblright{}) plus this root — the one who points out the law.

One word ties the chapter back to your first: a \textbf{valedictorian} is the person who says \emph{valē}, the farewell you learned in Chapter 1.

The Germanic branch kept the older sense. English \textbf{teach} descends from Old English \emph{tæcan}, \textquotedblleft{}to show,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{token} from \emph{tācen}, \textquotedblleft{}a sign\textquotedblright{} — both from the same root as \emph{dīcō}. Greek \emph{deíknumi} (\textquotedblleft{}I show\textquotedblright{}) gives \textbf{paradigm}, literally \textquotedblleft{}a thing shown side by side.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dīcō\textquotedblright{} — I say, with a hard c
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dīcis, dīcit\textquotedblright{} — you say, he or she says
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dīcimus, dīcitis, dīcunt\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — dictionary, verdict, predict, teach
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I say\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Dīcō}, hard c.) \textquotedblleft{}They say\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Dīcunt}.) What did the root originally mean? (\textbf{To point out, to show}.) What does a \textbf{valedictorian} literally do? (\textbf{Says valē}, the farewell.) Which everyday English verb keeps the old \textquotedblleft{}show\textquotedblright{} sense? (\textbf{Teach}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[videō, vidēre]{videō — where seeing and knowing were the same act}

\label{lesson:LA-C37-video}



\begin{quote}
You can already promise \textbf{crās tē vidēbō}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow I shall see you.\textquotedblright{} The verb inside that promise deserves its own lesson: it has the widest family of any word in this chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: videō — \textquotedblleft{}I see\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Videō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I see}.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{vidēre}. The \emph{v} is again a \emph{w}-sound, so this is \emph{WEE-day-oh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{videō} — I see
  \item \textbf{vidēs} — you see, to one person
  \item \textbf{videt} — he sees, she sees
  \item \textbf{vidēmus} — we see
  \item \textbf{vidētis} — you see, to several people
  \item \textbf{vident} — they see
\end{itemize}

The future you already know, \textbf{vidēbō} (\textquotedblleft{}I shall see\textquotedblright{}), is built on this same stem.

\begin{cousinweb}
The Proto-Indo-European root \emph{\textbf{*weyd-}} meant both \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} and, by the obvious step, \textquotedblleft{}to know\textquotedblright{} — because what you have seen, you know.

The Latin harvest is enormous. Plain derivatives give \textbf{vision}, \textbf{visible}, \textbf{video}, \textbf{visit}, and \textbf{vista}. Prefixed ones are richer: \textbf{evident} (\emph{ē-}, \textquotedblleft{}seen out, unmissable\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{provide} and \textbf{provision} (\emph{prō-}, \textquotedblleft{}to see ahead\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{prudent}, which is simply \emph{prōvidēns} worn down. \textbf{Survey} is \emph{super} plus \emph{vidēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to look over\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{review} and \textbf{revise} look again; \textbf{advice} is what you are shown. \textbf{Envy} is the sourest of them: \emph{invidēre} meant \textquotedblleft{}to look against,\textquotedblright{} to cast an eye upon what belongs to someone else.

The other branches keep the knowing half. English \textbf{wit}, \textbf{wise}, and \textbf{wisdom} are Germanic outcomes of the same root. Greek turned it into \emph{idéa} (\textquotedblleft{}the look of a thing\textquotedblright{}) — English \textbf{idea} — and into \emph{hístōr} (\textquotedblleft{}one who knows because he has seen\textquotedblright{}), giving \textbf{history} and \textbf{story}. Sanskrit made it \textbf{Veda}, \textquotedblleft{}knowledge.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}videō\textquotedblright{} — I see, with a w-sound
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vidēs, videt\textquotedblright{} — you see, he or she sees
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vidēmus, vidētis, vident\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — vision, evident, provide, survey, envy
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I see\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Videō}, with a w-sound.) \textquotedblleft{}They see\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Vident}.) What second meaning did the root carry besides \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{To know}.) What does \textbf{envy} literally describe? (\textbf{Looking against} someone.) Which English word for wisdom comes from this root? (\textbf{Wit}, and with it \emph{wise} and \emph{wisdom}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sciō, scīre]{sciō — the knowing that cuts things apart}

\label{lesson:LA-C37-scio}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Videō} already carried a shade of \textquotedblleft{}know.\textquotedblright{} Latin nevertheless keeps two dedicated verbs for knowing, and this lesson takes the first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sciō — \textquotedblleft{}I know\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Sciō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I know}\textquotedblright{} — know a fact, know that something is so. The dictionary form is \textbf{scīre}. The \emph{sc} is a plain \emph{sk}, so this is \emph{SKEE-oh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{sciō} — I know
  \item \textbf{scīs} — you know, to one person
  \item \textbf{scit} — he knows, she knows
  \item \textbf{scīmus} — we know
  \item \textbf{scītis} — you know, to several people
  \item \textbf{sciunt} — they know
\end{itemize}

Its negative is a single word: \textbf{nesciō}, \textquotedblleft{}I do not know\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ne} plus \emph{sciō}, fused. That is a genuinely useful thing to be able to say.

Latin's other knowing verb is \textbf{nōscō}, \textquotedblleft{}to get to know, to recognise.\textquotedblright{} A Roman used \emph{sciō} for knowing a fact and \emph{nōscō} for becoming acquainted.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Scīre} is generally traced to the Proto-Indo-European root \emph{\textbf{*skey-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to cut, to split\textquotedblright{} — knowing as the act of telling one thing from another. The link is the standard account rather than a certainty, and careful dictionaries mark it as probable. The same root gives Greek \emph{skhízein}, \textquotedblleft{}to split,\textquotedblright{} behind \textbf{schism} and \textbf{schizo-}, and English \textbf{shed} in its old sense of dividing.

From \emph{scīre} directly: \textbf{science} and \textbf{scientific} (\emph{scientia}, \textquotedblleft{}knowledge\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{conscience} and \textbf{conscious} (\emph{con-}, \textquotedblleft{}knowing with\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{omniscient} (\textquotedblleft{}all-knowing\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{prescient}. A \textbf{plebiscite} is a \emph{plēbis scītum}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing the people have decided.\textquotedblright{}

The prize of the family is \textbf{nice}. It comes from \emph{nescius}, \textquotedblleft{}not knowing,\textquotedblright{} which passed into Old French as \emph{nice}, \textquotedblleft{}simple, foolish,\textquotedblright{} then drifted through \textquotedblleft{}fussy\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}delicate\textquotedblright{} to today's mild compliment.

Now the false friend, and it is a big one. English \textbf{know} is \textbf{not} related to \emph{sciō}. It descends from \emph{\textbf{*ǵneh\textsubscript{3}-}}, the root behind Latin \textbf{nōscō} — the source of \textbf{notice}, \textbf{notion}, \textbf{cognition}, \textbf{recognise}, and \textbf{ignore}, and of Greek \emph{gnōsis} in \textbf{diagnosis}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sciō\textquotedblright{} — I know, opening sk-
  \item \textquotedblleft{}scīs, scit\textquotedblright{} — you know, he or she knows
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nesciō\textquotedblright{} — I do not know
  \item the English relatives — science, conscience, nice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I know\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Sciō}.) \textquotedblleft{}I do not know\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Nesciō}.) What older sense probably sits under the root? (\textbf{To cut or separate} — telling one thing from another.) Which mild English compliment began as \emph{nescius}, \textquotedblleft{}not knowing\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Nice}.) Is English \emph{know} from this verb? (\textbf{No} — from the root behind \emph{nōscō}, which gives \emph{notice} and \emph{cognition}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dō, dare]{dō — the eighth verb, and the whole set together}

\label{lesson:LA-C37-do}



\begin{quote}
Seven verbs so far: to be, to have, to go, to come, to say, to see, to know. One remains, and then the set closes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dō — \textquotedblleft{}I give\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Dō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I give}.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{dare}, and the \emph{a} in it is short — \emph{DAH-reh}, not \emph{DAH-ray}. That short vowel is unusual and marks \emph{dare} out as irregular.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{dō} — I give
  \item \textbf{dās} — you give, to one person
  \item \textbf{dat} — he gives, she gives
  \item \textbf{damus} — we give
  \item \textbf{datis} — you give, to several people
  \item \textbf{dant} — they give
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*deh\textsubscript{3}-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to give.\textquotedblright{} From the noun \emph{dōnum} (\textquotedblleft{}a gift\textquotedblright{}) English takes \textbf{donate}, \textbf{donor}, \textbf{condone}, and \textbf{pardon} (\emph{per-dōnāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to give thoroughly, to forgive\textquotedblright{}).

From the participle \emph{datum}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing given,\textquotedblright{} come \textbf{data} and \textbf{dative}, the giving case — and also \textbf{date}. A Roman letter closed with \emph{data Rōmae}, \textquotedblleft{}given at Rome,\textquotedblright{} followed by the day; the word for \textquotedblleft{}given\textquotedblright{} became the word for the day itself.

\emph{Trāns} plus \emph{dare} makes \emph{trādere}, \textquotedblleft{}to hand over,\textquotedblright{} and that single compound splits into \textbf{tradition} (handed down), \textbf{traitor} and \textbf{treason} (handed over to the enemy), \textbf{betray}, and \textbf{extradite}. \emph{Dōs}, \emph{dōtis} (\textquotedblleft{}dowry\textquotedblright{}) gives \textbf{dowry} and \textbf{endow}. Greek \emph{dídōmi} supplies \textbf{dose} and \textbf{anecdote} (\textquotedblleft{}things not given out\textquotedblright{}).

Two flags. English \textbf{give} is not from this root, despite the matching sense — it is Germanic and separate. And Latin compounds ending in \emph{-dere} — \emph{addere} (\textquotedblleft{}to add\textquotedblright{}), \emph{condere} (\textquotedblleft{}to found\textquotedblright{}) — belong to a \textbf{different} root, \emph{\textbf{*d\textsuperscript{h}eh\textsubscript{1}-}} (\textquotedblleft{}to put\textquotedblright{}), the one behind Greek \emph{títhēmi} and English \textbf{theme} and \textbf{thesis}. So \textbf{add} is not a relative of \emph{dare}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dō, dās, dat\textquotedblright{} — I give, you give, he or she gives
  \item the eight \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms — sum, habeō, eō, veniō, dīcō, videō, sciō, dō
  \item the eight \textquotedblleft{}he or she\textquotedblright{} forms — est, habet, it, venit, dīcit, videt, scit, dat
  \item the English relatives of dare — donate, data, date, tradition
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the eight \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms of this chapter. (\textbf{Sum, habeō, eō, veniō, dīcō, videō, sciō, dō}.) Now the eight \textquotedblleft{}he or she\textquotedblright{} forms. (\textbf{Est, habet, it, venit, dīcit, videt, scit, dat}.) Which English words come from \emph{datum}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing given\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Data}, \textbf{dative}, and \textbf{date}.) What does \emph{trādere} literally mean? (\textbf{To hand over} — hence \emph{tradition} and \emph{traitor}.) Is English \emph{give} a relative? (\textbf{No.})
\end{tcolorbox}
